## From the 16th Century to the Digital Age: The Documented History of Bell-Ringing

The earliest written records mentioning the use of bells in Almuñécar appear in the chapter acts and the account books of the Parish of la Encarnación, whose oldest preserved archives date back to the mid-16th century. In those pages, the sacristans meticulously recorded the payments received for ringing for the council, tolling for the dead, or pealing for the festivities of the liturgical calendar. This was no mere decorative trade: the bell-ringer was both a municipal and ecclesiastical employee, with duties outlined in ordinances that regulated everything from the number of strikes to the exact duration of each ring.

The municipal archives of Almuñécar preserve indirect references to those ordinances in the council minutes, where such prosaic matters as the maintenance of ropes, the purchase of clappers, or the repair of bell towers damaged by storms were debated. The documentation reveals that the ringing served a triple function: it summoned the residents to open council meetings, marked the rhythms of the working day, and warned of dangers such as fires, storms, or incursions by Berber pirates, a constant threat on the coast of Granada during the 16th and 17th centuries. Each of these warnings had a distinct rhythmic pattern, and its correct execution could mean the difference between calm and collective panic.

Comparing this with other localities helps to gauge the antiquity of the craft. The bell-ringers' gathering in Villavante, in the province of León, has been held uninterruptedly for thirty-nine years, a respectable figure that nevertheless pales in comparison to the more than four centuries of documented bell-ringing in Almuñécar. This longevity does not imply stagnation: the craft has evolved in its techniques, repertoires, and meanings, adapting to the needs of each era. What in the 16th century was an essential communication system for survival, in the 19th became a marker of local identity, and in the 20th began to be perceived as a relic of the past.

The turning point came in the 1960s, when the electrification of bell towers began to take hold in most Spanish municipalities. In Almuñécar, as in so many others, motors replaced hands and programmable clocks replaced the sacristans who climbed the tower several times a day. Automation promised regularity, savings, and a precision that the human touch could not always guarantee.

But with it, something harder to quantify was lost: the ability to improvise nuances, to adjust the intensity of the strike to the mood of the town, to differentiate a peal for a major feast from one for a minor feast with variations that no motor could reproduce. The parish account books of that era record the entries for the installation of the first electric mechanisms, alongside the final wage payments for manual bell-ringers.

Some of these men continued to climb the tower for years, not because it was necessary, but because they refused to abandon a craft they had inherited from their fathers and grandfathers. The parish records do not capture their names with the detail they deserved, but they do bear witness to a silent transition: the replacement of a human language with a mechanical hum that sounded the same at baptisms as at funerals.

Historical documentation also allows us to reconstruct the sonic geography of the municipality. It was not the same to hear the large bell of la Encarnación, reserved for solemn announcements and death knells for illustrious figures, as the smaller bell of the convent or the small bells of the hermitages scattered throughout the municipal district. Each had a specific timbre, range, and function, and the locals knew how to distinguish them without needing to see the tower. This auditory cartography, which today can barely be glimpsed in the documents, constitutes one of the most fragile intangible heritages of Almuñécar.

Notarial archives add another layer of information, and by no means a minor one. In the wills and marriage contracts of the 17th and 18th centuries, there appear bequests intended to pay for bell-ringing for the soul of the deceased, with precise instructions on the number of peals and the required solemnity. These seemingly minor clauses demonstrate just how deeply the sound of the bells was embedded in the social and spiritual contract of the community. To die without a proper toll was, for many, a way of dying twice: once on earth and once in the memory of the living.

The digital age has added a new chapter to this story, and not a particularly reassuring one. Current systems allow the ringing to be programmed from a mobile phone, the volume to be adjusted, traditional peals to be simulated, and even pre-recorded sounds to be played without anyone needing to set foot in the bell tower. The paradox is evident: it has never been easier to make a bell ring, and there have never been fewer people capable of truly ringing it. The technology that promised to preserve the sound has ended up emptying it of meaning, turning a language into a mere acoustic notification.

Local historians who have worked with the parish and municipal archives of Almuñécar agree on one point: the documentation exists, it is abundant, and it allows for a remarkably precise reconstruction of the evolution of manual bell-ringing from the 16th century to the present day. What is lacking is the generational handover that turns that archival knowledge into living practice. Papers can wait in files for centuries, but the hands that know how to interpret what those papers describe are fading away one by one, without anyone yet having found a way to pass on what cannot be learned by reading.
